case: A 68-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of a deep, aching pain in his right hip and pelvis that is worse at night. He has also noticed that his hats no longer fit. Physical examination shows frontal bossing and warm skin over the right anterior thigh. Laboratory studies show: calcium 9.6 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5), phosphate 3.4 mg/dL (2.5 to 4.5), alkaline phosphatase 410 U/L (40 to 130), and parathyroid hormone 38 pg/mL (10 to 65). Radiographs show a thickened cortex and coarse trabeculae in the right hemipelvis and proximal femur, and patchy areas of increased density in the skull. Diagnosis: Paget disease of bone.

questions.stem: A bone biopsy is taken from the right iliac crest. Which of the following histologic findings is most likely?
options: Mosaic of lamellar bone joined by irregular cement lines
Wide seams of unmineralized osteoid covering normal trabeculae
Thin, widely spaced trabeculae with normal mineralization
Trabeculae with retained cores of calcified cartilage
approach: Notice an older man with bone pain, enlarging skull, and an isolated high alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium, phosphate, and PTH.
That pattern points to Paget disease, a disorder of disorganized remodeling.
Predict the tissue result: repeated rounds of resorption and hasty repair leave a mosaic of lamellar bone.
questions.why: Paget disease starts with overactive, oversized osteoclasts that resorb bone. Osteoblasts then lay down new bone quickly and in a disorganized way. The many rounds of resorption and repair leave lamellar bone pieces joined by irregular cement lines, the classic mosaic pattern. The bone is thick but weak, and the high osteoblast activity raises alkaline phosphatase while calcium, phosphate, and PTH stay normal.
whyNot: Correct.
Excess unmineralized osteoid is the hallmark of osteomalacia from vitamin D deficiency. That causes low or low-normal calcium and phosphate with high PTH, which this patient does not have.
This is osteoporosis: less bone of normal quality. Osteoporosis does not thicken the cortex, enlarge the skull, or raise alkaline phosphatase on its own.
Retained cartilage cores reflect failed osteoclast resorption in osteopetrosis. Paget disease is the opposite at the start, with too much osteoclast activity.

topics: Paget disease phases and mosaic bone

questions.stem: Two years later, he reports shortness of breath on exertion. His pulse is 104/min and bounding, and the skin over the affected pelvis and skull is warm. Echocardiography shows a cardiac output of 9.5 L/min (4 to 8) with normal valves. Which of the following best explains these cardiac findings?
options: Systemic hypertension from calcification of large arteries
Anemia from replacement of marrow by fibrous tissue
Arteriovenous shunting through hypervascular pagetic bone
Hypercalcemia shortening the ventricular action potential
approach: Link warm skin over pagetic bone to increased blood flow through that bone.
Recall that very vascular pagetic bone acts like many small arteriovenous fistulas.
Low resistance lowers afterload and raises venous return, so the heart must pump a high output, which can lead to high-output failure.
questions.why: In active Paget disease the remodeling bone and its marrow become highly vascular. When much of the skeleton is involved, the blood flowing through these beds acts like arteriovenous shunts. Systemic vascular resistance falls, venous return rises, and the heart responds with a high output and wide pulse pressure. Over time this load can produce high-output heart failure.
whyNot: Arterial stiffening raises afterload and causes pressure overload. It does not raise cardiac output or warm the skin over the bones.
Severe anemia can cause high-output failure, but Paget disease does not typically cause marrow failure. Fibrous marrow in Paget disease is local, not widespread enough to cause anemia.
Correct.
His calcium is normal. Hypercalcemia shortens the QT interval but does not raise cardiac output.

questions.stem: Over the next year he develops left-sided sensorineural hearing loss and weakness of all the muscles of facial expression on the left. Narrowing of which of the following openings by thickened bone best explains both findings?
options: Superior orbital fissure
Jugular foramen
Stylomastoid foramen
Internal acoustic meatus
approach: Name the nerves involved: facial weakness points to cranial nerve VII and sensorineural hearing loss to cranial nerve VIII.
Ask which skull opening carries both nerves together.
Cranial nerves VII and VIII enter the petrous temporal bone together through the internal acoustic meatus.
questions.why: Cranial nerves VII and VIII leave the posterior cranial fossa together through the internal acoustic meatus in the petrous temporal bone. Thickening of the temporal bone in Paget disease can narrow this canal and compress both nerves. Hearing loss in Paget disease can also be conductive from involvement of the ossicles, but the combination with facial weakness places the lesion at the meatus.
whyNot: This fissure carries cranial nerves III, IV, V1, and VI to the orbit. Compression would cause eye movement problems and forehead numbness, not hearing loss or facial weakness.
The jugular foramen carries cranial nerves IX, X, and XI and the internal jugular vein. Compression would cause swallowing and voice problems and trapezius weakness.
Only the facial nerve exits here. Compression could cause facial weakness, but it could not explain sensorineural hearing loss.
Correct.

questions.stem: He falls and fractures his left femoral shaft and is kept on bed rest for 3 weeks. His serum calcium rises to 11.8 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5). Which of the following sets of hormone changes is most likely?
options: High PTH and high calcitriol
Low PTH and low calcitriol
Low PTH and high calcitriol
High PTH and low calcitriol
approach: Identify the source of the extra calcium: immobilization speeds osteoclast resorption, and pagetic bone already turns over fast.
Calcium-sensing receptors on the parathyroid glands respond to the high calcium by cutting PTH secretion.
Without PTH, renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase is not stimulated, so calcitriol falls.
questions.why: Bed rest removes the mechanical loading that keeps bone formation and resorption balanced, and resorption wins. In a patient whose bone already turns over rapidly, this can release enough calcium to cause hypercalcemia. The parathyroid glands sense high calcium and lower PTH. PTH normally stimulates 1-alpha-hydroxylase in the proximal tubule, so calcitriol also falls. This is a PTH-independent hypercalcemia.
whyNot: This pattern is seen in primary hyperparathyroidism, where PTH drives the hypercalcemia. Here the calcium comes from bone resorption, so PTH should be suppressed.
Correct.
High calcitriol with low PTH occurs when calcitriol is made outside the kidney, as in sarcoidosis. Bed rest does not do this, and without PTH the renal enzyme is not stimulated.
High PTH with low calcitriol occurs in chronic kidney disease, where the kidney cannot make calcitriol. Calcium is usually low or normal in that setting.

dx: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head in SLE treated with glucocorticoids
case: A 32-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of right groin pain that is worse with walking. For the past 2 years she has taken prednisone 20 to 40 mg daily for lupus nephritis. She does not drink alcohol. Physical examination shows pain and limited range of motion on internal rotation of the right hip. Radiographs of the hip are normal. MRI shows a band of low signal intensity outlining a wedge of subchondral bone in the anterosuperior right femoral head, with no collapse. Diagnosis: avascular necrosis of the right femoral head related to glucocorticoid therapy and SLE.

questions.stem: A core decompression is performed, and tissue from the lesion is examined. Which of the following histologic findings is most likely?
options: Trabeculae with empty osteocyte lacunae and necrotic marrow fat
Mosaic lamellar bone with irregular cement lines and fibrovascular marrow
A fragment of dead bone surrounded by neutrophils and reactive new bone
Wide seams of unmineralized osteoid lining the trabeculae
approach: Recognize avascular necrosis as an infarct of bone and marrow from interrupted blood flow.
Ask what dead bone looks like: osteocytes die and leave empty lacunae, and marrow fat undergoes necrosis.
Choose the option that shows ischemic cell death without infection or a remodeling disorder.
questions.why: Avascular necrosis is ischemic death of bone and marrow. Osteocytes die and their lacunae are left empty, and the marrow fat becomes necrotic. The dead subchondral bone cannot remodel well, so it can fracture and collapse, flattening the joint surface. Glucocorticoids, alcohol, SLE, sickle cell disease, decompression sickness, and femoral neck or scaphoid fractures are classic causes, and the femoral head is the most common site because its retinacular arteries have few collaterals.
whyNot: Correct.
This is Paget disease, which comes from disordered remodeling, not loss of blood supply. It occurs in older adults with high alkaline phosphatase.
A sequestrum with an involucrum is the picture of chronic osteomyelitis. That needs infection, and she has no fever or other signs of infection.
Wide osteoid seams mean poor mineralization, as in osteomalacia. Bone cells stay alive in osteomalacia.

questions.stem: Three years before her hip pain began, she had pain and swelling in the small joints of both hands. Which of the following findings in her hands is most likely?
options: Marginal bony erosions of the metacarpophalangeal joints
Pencil-in-cup deformities of the distal joints
Sclerodactyly with fingertip calcinosis
Reducible deformities without erosions on radiographs
approach: Recall the typical arthritis of SLE: symmetric small-joint polyarthritis.
Lupus synovitis does not erode bone; its deformities come from lax ligaments and joint capsules.
Pick the option that combines deformity with no erosions.
questions.why: Arthritis is one of the most common features of SLE and usually involves the small joints of the hands symmetrically, like rheumatoid arthritis. Lupus synovitis does not form the invasive pannus that erodes cartilage and bone in rheumatoid arthritis. Some patients develop ulnar deviation and swan-neck deformities from lax tendons and capsules, which can be pushed back into place and show no erosions on radiographs (Jaccoud arthropathy).
whyNot: Marginal erosions come from invasive pannus in rheumatoid arthritis. Lupus arthritis does not form an erosive pannus.
Pencil-in-cup erosions of the distal interphalangeal joints are typical of psoriatic arthritis, a seronegative spondyloarthropathy.
Tight, thickened skin over the fingers with calcium deposits is a feature of systemic sclerosis, not SLE.
Correct.

questions.stem: During flares of her lupus, serum C3 and C4 fall and anti-double-stranded DNA titers rise, and her joint symptoms worsen. Which of the following mechanisms best explains her joint inflammation during these flares?
options: Mast cell degranulation triggered by IgE cross-linking
Deposited circulating immune complexes that fix complement
Antibody binding to a fixed antigen on synovial lining cells
CD8+ T cells directly lysing muscle and synovial cells
approach: Link low C3 and C4 to complement consumption.
Link anti-dsDNA antibodies to circulating antigen-antibody complexes.
Complexes that lodge in tissue and activate complement define type III hypersensitivity.
questions.why: In SLE, antibodies bind nuclear antigens such as DNA to form circulating immune complexes. These complexes deposit in the synovium, skin, kidney, and vessel walls and activate the classical complement pathway, which consumes C3 and C4. Complement fragments such as C5a recruit neutrophils, which cause the inflammation. This is type III hypersensitivity, and falling complement with rising anti-dsDNA is a marker of active disease.
whyNot: This is type I hypersensitivity, as in allergic reactions. It does not consume C3 and C4 or involve anti-DNA antibodies.
Correct.
Antibody against a fixed tissue antigen is type II hypersensitivity, as in the polyarthritis of rheumatic fever. Anti-DNA antibodies form circulating complexes instead.
Direct T-cell killing is type IV hypersensitivity, as in polymyositis. It does not lower complement levels.

questions.stem: She also reports difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs. Examination shows symmetric weakness of the hip flexors and shoulder abductors without tenderness. Serum creatine kinase is 85 U/L (30 to 170). Which of the following findings on a muscle biopsy is most likely?
options: Fiber type grouping with groups of atrophic fibers
Endomysial CD8+ T cells with necrotic muscle fibers
Selective atrophy of type II fibers without necrosis
Perifascicular atrophy with perimysial inflammatory cells
approach: Notice proximal weakness with a normal creatine kinase in a patient on long-term glucocorticoids.
A normal CK argues against an inflammatory myopathy with fiber necrosis.
Glucocorticoid myopathy selectively shrinks type II (fast glycolytic) fibers.
questions.why: Long-term glucocorticoids cause a proximal myopathy that mainly affects the hip and shoulder girdles. Steroids increase muscle protein breakdown and reduce synthesis, and type II fast glycolytic fibers are the most affected. Because the fibers shrink but do not die, creatine kinase stays normal. Disuse causes the same type II atrophy pattern.
whyNot: Fiber type grouping and grouped atrophy follow denervation and reinnervation, as in motor neuron disease. Neurogenic weakness also brings fasciculations and is often distal.
This is polymyositis or lupus myositis. Active fiber necrosis releases creatine kinase, so CK would be high.
Correct.
Perifascicular atrophy is the hallmark of dermatomyositis, which raises CK and usually shows a skin rash.

case: A 41-year-old man comes to the physician because of an 8-month history of a slowly enlarging, painful mass over his left hip. Since childhood he has had multiple painless bony lumps near his knees, shoulders, and hips, and his father had similar lumps. Physical examination shows a firm, fixed mass over the left iliac wing and several hard, nontender bony prominences around both knees. Radiographs show multiple bony outgrowths from the metaphyses of long bones. MRI of the left ilium shows an outgrowth with a lobulated cartilage cap 4 cm thick. Biopsy shows a malignant cartilage-forming tumor. Diagnosis: secondary chondrosarcoma arising from an osteochondroma in hereditary multiple osteochondromas.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings in the resected tumor would most strongly support chondrosarcoma rather than osteosarcoma?
options: Pleomorphic spindle cells laying down lacelike osteoid directly
Sheets of small round blue cells with membranous CD99 staining
Mononuclear stromal cells mixed with osteoclast-like giant cells
Malignant chondrocytes in hyaline matrix with no tumor osteoid
approach: Recall that bone sarcomas are named for the matrix the malignant cells make.
Chondrosarcoma cells make cartilage only; any osteoid made directly by tumor cells makes the tumor an osteosarcoma.
Choose the option with malignant cartilage and no tumor osteoid.
questions.why: Chondrosarcoma is a malignant tumor whose cells make hyaline or myxoid cartilage matrix but no osteoid. It is a tumor of middle-aged and older adults and favors the pelvis, proximal femur, and shoulder girdle. It may arise on its own, from an enchondroma, or in the cartilage cap of an osteochondroma, as here. A thick cap (more than about 2 cm in an adult) and new pain in an old lesion are warning signs of malignant change.
whyNot: Osteoid made directly by malignant cells defines osteosarcoma. Osteosarcoma can contain cartilage, but tumor osteoid places it in that category.
Small round blue cells with CD99 are Ewing sarcoma, a tumor of children and adolescents, usually in the diaphysis or pelvis.
This describes giant cell tumor of bone, an epiphyseal tumor of young adults that does not make cartilage.
Correct.

questions.stem: Genetic testing shows a germline loss-of-function mutation in EXT1. Which of the following best describes the lesions he has had around his knees since childhood?
options: Bony stalks continuous with the marrow cavity and capped by cartilage
Intramedullary nodules of hyaline cartilage in the bones of the hands
Small cortical nidus of osteoid surrounded by dense reactive bone
Expansile lytic lesions of the epiphysis with thin cortical shells
approach: Recognize EXT1 or EXT2 mutations as the cause of hereditary multiple osteochondromas.
Recall the structure of an osteochondroma.
The cortex and marrow of the stalk are continuous with the parent bone, and a hyaline cartilage cap sits on top.
questions.why: EXT1 and EXT2 encode enzymes that make heparan sulfate, which helps control growth-plate signaling. Loss of both copies in growth-plate chondrocytes lets cartilage grow out sideways from the metaphysis, forming an osteochondroma. The lesion is a bony stalk whose cortex and marrow are continuous with the parent bone, covered by a cartilage cap. Solitary osteochondromas rarely turn malignant, but the risk of chondrosarcoma is higher in the hereditary multiple form.
whyNot: Correct.
This is enchondroma. Many enchondromas occur in Ollier disease and, with hemangiomas, in Maffucci syndrome; these are not caused by EXT mutations.
This is osteoid osteoma, a painful tumor of young people that is not hereditary and does not form a palpable bony lump.
Expansile epiphyseal lytic lesions suggest giant cell tumor of bone, which occurs in young adults after the growth plates close.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the main fibrillar collagen in the cartilage cap of the benign lesions around his knees?
options: Type I
Type II
Type III
Type IV
approach: Identify the tissue: the cap of an osteochondroma is hyaline cartilage, like a growth plate.
Match hyaline cartilage to its collagen type.
Hyaline cartilage and the nucleus pulposus are made mainly of type II collagen.
questions.why: The cap of an osteochondroma is hyaline cartilage that behaves like a growth plate, and its main collagen is type II. Type II collagen forms thin fibrils that hold proteoglycans such as aggrecan, giving cartilage its resistance to compression. Below the cap, the cartilage undergoes endochondral ossification into the type I collagen bone of the stalk.
whyNot: Type I collagen is the main collagen of bone, tendon, ligament, and fibrocartilage. It forms the bony stalk of an osteochondroma, not the cap.
Correct.
Type III collagen forms reticular fibers and is abundant in blood vessel walls and early granulation tissue.
Type IV collagen is a network-forming collagen of basement membranes, not a fibrillar collagen of cartilage.

questions.stem: A second outgrowth on the neck of his right fibula enlarges. He develops right foot drop. Which of the following additional findings is most likely?
options: Weak plantar flexion and numbness on the sole of the foot
Weak knee extension and numbness on the medial leg
Weak foot eversion and numbness on the dorsum of the foot
Weak hip adduction and numbness on the medial thigh
approach: Locate the lesion: the neck of the fibula.
The common fibular nerve wraps around the fibular neck, where it is exposed to compression and fracture.
Predict its deficits: the deep branch supplies dorsiflexors and the superficial branch supplies evertors and most of the dorsal foot skin.
questions.why: The common fibular (peroneal) nerve winds around the lateral side of the fibular neck just under the skin, so masses, fractures, and casts there can compress it. Its deep branch supplies the anterior compartment dorsiflexors, so injury causes foot drop. Its superficial branch supplies the lateral compartment evertors and the skin of most of the dorsum of the foot, so eversion is weak and that skin is numb.
whyNot: These are signs of tibial nerve injury. The tibial nerve runs deep in the posterior leg, away from the fibular neck.
These point to the femoral nerve and its saphenous branch, which do not pass near the fibula.
Correct.
These are obturator nerve signs. The obturator nerve supplies the medial thigh and runs nowhere near the fibula.

case: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 6-week history of pain and swelling of the left thigh. He has had intermittent fevers and has lost 3 kg (6.6 lb). His temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F). Physical examination shows a tender, warm mass over the mid left thigh. Leukocyte count is 12,800/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 58 mm/h (0 to 15). A radiograph shows a permeative lytic lesion in the femoral diaphysis with layered, onion-skin periosteal new bone and a large soft tissue mass. Blood cultures are negative. Biopsy shows sheets of uniform small round blue cells. Molecular testing confirms Ewing sarcoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following immunohistochemical staining patterns is most likely in this tumor?
options: Nuclear myogenin with strong cytoplasmic desmin
Membranous CD99 with negative myogenin
Strong membranous CD45 with negative CD99
Cytoplasmic synaptophysin with negative CD99
approach: List the small round blue cell tumors of childhood: Ewing sarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, lymphoma, and neuroblastoma.
A diaphyseal bone tumor with onion-skin periosteum, fever, and high ESR in a teenager fits Ewing sarcoma.
Ewing sarcoma cells show strong membranous CD99 and lack muscle, leukocyte, and neuroendocrine markers.
questions.why: Ewing sarcoma is a tumor of children and adolescents made of sheets of uniform small round blue cells. It usually arises in the diaphysis of long bones or in the pelvis, and the periosteum lifts in layers to form onion-skin new bone. Strong membranous CD99 staining supports the diagnosis, and the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion from t(11;22) confirms it. Fever, leukocytosis, and a high ESR are common and can mimic osteomyelitis, which is why biopsy and cultures matter.
whyNot: Myogenin and desmin mark skeletal muscle differentiation in rhabdomyosarcoma, another small round blue cell tumor of children, usually in the head and neck or genitourinary tract.
Correct.
CD45 is the common leukocyte antigen. A CD45-positive small round cell tumor is a lymphoma.
Synaptophysin marks neuroendocrine tumors such as neuroblastoma, which usually arises in the adrenal medulla of young children.

questions.stem: Molecular testing shows a t(11;22)(q24;q12) translocation. Which of the following best describes the product of this rearrangement?
options: A constitutively active cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase
An anti-apoptotic protein overexpressed from an immunoglobulin promoter
A truncated tumor suppressor that can no longer bind E2F
A chimeric transcription factor that activates abnormal target genes
approach: Recall the genes at the breakpoints: EWSR1 on chromosome 22 and FLI1 on chromosome 11.
FLI1 is an ETS family transcription factor.
The fusion joins the EWSR1 activation domain to the FLI1 DNA-binding domain, making a new transcription factor.
questions.why: The t(11;22) translocation fuses the EWSR1 gene on chromosome 22 to FLI1 on chromosome 11. The fusion protein keeps the DNA-binding domain of FLI1, an ETS family transcription factor, and gains a strong activation region from EWSR1. It binds DNA and turns on a set of genes that drive growth and block normal differentiation. Detecting this fusion confirms the diagnosis.
whyNot: A fused, always-on tyrosine kinase is the product of BCR-ABL1 from t(9;22) in chronic myeloid leukemia.
Moving BCL2 next to the immunoglobulin heavy chain promoter by t(14;18) causes follicular lymphoma.
Loss of RB function frees E2F and drives osteosarcoma and retinoblastoma. It is a loss of a tumor suppressor, not a fusion gene.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following embryonic tissues gives rise to the bone in which this tumor arose?
options: Sclerotome of the paraxial mesoderm
Neural crest mesenchyme
Somatic layer of lateral plate mesoderm
Intermediate mesoderm of the nephrogenic cord
approach: Identify the bone: the femur, part of the appendicular skeleton.
Recall that limb buds grow out from the body wall, which is lined by the somatic layer of lateral plate mesoderm.
Limb bones, cartilage, and tendons come from this layer; somites supply limb muscle instead.
questions.why: The limb buds form when somatic lateral plate mesoderm and its overlying ectoderm grow out from the body wall. This mesoderm forms the limb bones, cartilages, tendons, and ligaments. Limb muscles come from myotome cells that migrate in from the somites. The axial skeleton comes from sclerotome, and most of the facial skeleton comes from neural crest.
whyNot: Sclerotome forms the vertebrae and ribs, the axial skeleton. Limb bones do not come from somites.
Neural crest mesenchyme forms much of the bone and cartilage of the face and anterior skull, not the limbs.
Correct.
Intermediate mesoderm forms the kidneys and gonads and does not form bone.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how the region of the femur where this tumor arose first ossified during development?
options: A primary center within a hyaline cartilage model
A secondary center within a hyaline cartilage model
Direct ossification within a sheet of mesenchyme
Cavitation of interzone mesenchyme
approach: Locate the tumor: the femoral diaphysis.
Recall that long bones form by endochondral ossification on a hyaline cartilage model.
The first, or primary, ossification center appears in the diaphysis before birth.
questions.why: The femur forms by endochondral ossification. Mesenchyme first makes a hyaline cartilage model. Early in development a periosteal bone collar forms around the middle of the shaft, the central cartilage calcifies, and blood vessels bring in osteoprogenitor cells to form the primary ossification center in the diaphysis. Secondary centers appear later in the epiphyses, and the growth plate between them allows lengthening.
whyNot: Correct.
Secondary ossification centers form in the epiphyses, mostly around birth or after. The tumor is in the shaft.
Intramembranous ossification forms the flat bones of the skull vault and most of the clavicle, not the femoral shaft.
Cavitation of interzone mesenchyme creates synovial joint cavities. It does not make bone.

case: A 17-year-old boy comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of pain in his right shin. The pain is worst at night and wakes him from sleep. It goes away within an hour of taking ibuprofen. He has no fever or weight loss. Physical examination shows mild tenderness over the anterior right tibia without swelling or warmth. Leukocyte count and erythrocyte sedimentation rate are within normal limits. CT shows a round 1.2 cm lucent nidus within the anterior cortex of the tibial diaphysis, surrounded by dense sclerotic bone. Diagnosis: osteoid osteoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the pattern of his pain and its response to ibuprofen?
options: Neutrophils in the nidus release leukotriene B4
Osteoclasts in the sclerotic rim release bradykinin locally
Prostaglandin E2 made by cyclooxygenase in the nidus
Mast cells around the nidus release histamine
approach: Note the classic history: night pain from a small cortical lesion that is relieved by NSAIDs.
NSAIDs work by blocking cyclooxygenase.
So the pain must depend on a cyclooxygenase product, prostaglandin E2 made by the nidus.
questions.why: Osteoid osteoma is a benign bone-forming tumor under about 2 cm, usually in the cortex of the femur or tibia of adolescents and young men. The nidus of osteoid and woven bone makes large amounts of prostaglandin E2, which causes the pain. NSAIDs block cyclooxygenase and so relieve the pain dramatically. Osteoblastoma has similar tissue but is larger than 2 cm, favors the vertebrae, and its pain is not relieved by NSAIDs.
whyNot: Leukotrienes come from the lipoxygenase pathway, which NSAIDs do not block. The nidus is not a neutrophilic abscess.
Bradykinin is made from kininogen by kallikrein in plasma, and NSAIDs do not block its production.
Correct.
Histamine release is not blocked by NSAIDs, and the nidus is not a mast cell lesion.

questions.stem: The nidus is made of irregular trabeculae of woven bone rimmed by osteoblasts. Compared with the normal lamellar bone of the surrounding cortex, which of the following features best describes woven bone?
options: Concentric lamellae around central vascular canals
Randomly oriented collagen with more osteocytes per volume
Parallel collagen sheets that change direction in each layer
Fewer osteocytes with greater resistance to bending
approach: Recall that woven bone is the first bone made in development, fracture repair, and fast-growing lesions.
It is laid down quickly, so its collagen is disorganized and many osteoblasts are trapped as osteocytes.
Lamellar bone is laid down slowly in ordered layers and forms osteons in compact bone.
questions.why: Woven bone is immature bone made quickly. Its collagen fibers run in random directions, it contains more osteocytes, and it is less mineralized and weaker than lamellar bone. Lamellar bone has collagen in orderly layers. In compact bone, these lamellae form osteons around Haversian canals, with osteocytes in lacunae connected by canaliculi and Volkmann canals linking the osteons. In adults, woven bone points to rapid bone formation such as a healing fracture, Paget disease, or a bone-forming tumor.
whyNot: Concentric lamellae around a Haversian canal form an osteon, the unit of mature compact lamellar bone.
Correct.
Collagen in parallel sheets that alternate direction between layers is the structure of lamellar bone and gives it strength.
Woven bone is weaker than lamellar bone, not stronger, and it has more osteocytes, not fewer.

questions.stem: Giant cell tumor of bone was included in the radiologist's differential diagnosis. In giant cell tumor of bone, which of the following cell populations are the neoplastic cells?
options: Multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells with RANK
Synovial cells that overexpress CSF1
Osteoblasts that secrete prostaglandin E2
Mononuclear stromal cells that express RANKL
approach: Recall giant cell tumor of bone: an epiphyseal, soap-bubble lytic lesion in young adults.
The striking giant cells are osteoclast-like cells, but they are not the tumor cells.
The neoplastic mononuclear stromal cells express RANKL, which recruits and activates the giant cells.
questions.why: Giant cell tumor of bone is a locally aggressive tumor of the epiphysis in young adults, usually around the knee, and appears as an expansile soap-bubble lytic lesion. The neoplastic cells are mononuclear stromal cells that express RANKL. RANKL binds RANK on monocyte precursors and drives them to fuse into the osteoclast-like giant cells that destroy bone. This is why the RANKL-blocking antibody denosumab can shrink these tumors.
whyNot: The giant cells are reactive. They are recruited and activated by RANKL from the stromal cells, and they cause the bone destruction.
CSF1 overexpression drives tenosynovial giant cell tumor, which arises from synovium or tendon sheaths, not inside bone.
Prostaglandin-secreting osteoblasts describe the nidus of this patient's osteoid osteoma.
Correct.

questions.stem: Osteoblasts in the nidus secrete osteocalcin, a protein that binds the mineral phase of bone. Which of the following post-translational modifications allows osteocalcin to bind this mineral?
options: Gamma-carboxylation of glutamate, requiring vitamin K
Hydroxylation of proline residues, requiring vitamin C
Oxidative deamination of lysine, requiring copper
Phosphorylation of serine, requiring magnesium
approach: Identify the mineral of bone: calcium hydroxyapatite.
Calcium-binding proteins such as clotting factors and osteocalcin use gamma-carboxyglutamate residues to bind calcium.
Gamma-carboxylation needs reduced vitamin K as a cofactor.
questions.why: Osteocalcin is made by osteoblasts and is one of the most abundant noncollagen proteins in bone. Vitamin K dependent gamma-glutamyl carboxylase adds a second carboxyl group to specific glutamate residues. These gamma-carboxyglutamate residues bind calcium and let osteocalcin attach to hydroxyapatite. The same modification activates clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, which is why warfarin can also lower carboxylated osteocalcin.
whyNot: Correct.
Prolyl hydroxylation stabilizes the collagen triple helix. Its loss in vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, not a defect in calcium binding by osteocalcin.
Copper-dependent lysyl oxidase forms the cross-links that strengthen collagen and elastin. It does not modify osteocalcin.
Magnesium supports kinases and PTH secretion, but the calcium-binding residues of osteocalcin come from carboxylation, not phosphorylation.

dx: Osteosarcoma of the distal femur after hereditary retinoblastoma
case: A 15-year-old girl comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of pain and swelling above her right knee. She was treated for bilateral retinoblastoma in infancy. Physical examination shows a firm, tender mass over the distal right thigh. Serum alkaline phosphatase is 520 U/L (for age, about 50 to 260). A radiograph shows a destructive, mixed lytic and sclerotic lesion in the distal femoral metaphysis with a triangle of elevated periosteum at its edge and radiating spicules of new bone in the soft tissue. Biopsy shows pleomorphic malignant cells producing lacelike osteoid. Diagnosis: osteosarcoma.

questions.stem: This tumor has a second, smaller age peak later in life. Which of the following groups is at increased risk for this tumor in later adulthood?
options: Adults with hereditary multiple osteochondromas
Older adults with Paget disease of bone
Adults with multiple enchondromas
Older adults with long-standing gout
approach: Recall the bimodal age pattern of osteosarcoma: adolescents during the growth spurt and older adults.
In older adults, osteosarcoma usually follows a condition with high bone turnover or DNA damage.
Paget disease and prior radiation are the classic predisposing conditions.
questions.why: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignant bone tumor apart from myeloma. Its main peak is in adolescents, where it arises in the metaphysis around the knee during the growth spurt. A second, smaller peak occurs in older adults, usually on a background of Paget disease or previous radiation. The defining feature is osteoid made directly by malignant cells.
whyNot: Hereditary multiple osteochondromas raise the risk of chondrosarcoma in the cartilage caps, not osteosarcoma.
Correct.
Multiple enchondromas in Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome raise the risk of chondrosarcoma.
Gout causes erosive arthritis and tophi but does not lead to bone sarcoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her increased risk for this tumor?
options: A second hit in RB1 that frees E2F to push cells into S phase
A gain-of-function RB1 mutation that keeps E2F tightly bound
A germline TP53 mutation that removes apoptosis after DNA damage
A somatic EWSR1-FLI1 fusion created by prior radiation exposure
approach: Bilateral retinoblastoma in infancy means a germline loss-of-function RB1 mutation in every cell.
Tumors arise when the second RB1 copy is lost in a cell, the two-hit model.
Without RB protein, E2F is free to drive the G1 to S transition.
questions.why: Children with hereditary retinoblastoma inherit or are born with one nonfunctional RB1 allele in every cell. When a bone cell loses the second allele, it has no working RB protein. RB normally binds E2F and holds the cell in G1 until cyclin D and CDK4/6 phosphorylate it. Without RB, E2F drives cells into S phase unchecked. Osteosarcoma is the most common second cancer in these patients. Its imaging shows a Codman triangle of lifted periosteum and a sunburst pattern of tumor bone, and it spreads through the blood to the lungs.
whyNot: Correct.
Bound E2F holds cells in G1, which would block growth. Retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma come from loss of RB function.
Germline TP53 loss in Li-Fraumeni syndrome also raises osteosarcoma risk, but her history of bilateral retinoblastoma points to a germline RB1 mutation.
EWSR1-FLI1 defines Ewing sarcoma, a small round cell tumor that does not make osteoid.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man comes to the physician because of back pain. Radiographs show multiple dense, sclerotic lesions in the lumbar vertebrae and pelvis. Which of the following is the most likely primary tumor?
options: Renal cell carcinoma
Follicular thyroid carcinoma
Prostatic adenocarcinoma
Squamous cell lung carcinoma
approach: In an older adult with multiple bone lesions, think of metastases before a primary bone tumor.
Classify the lesions: dense and sclerotic means osteoblastic.
Prostate cancer is the classic cause of osteoblastic metastases in men.
questions.why: Metastases are far more common than primary malignant bone tumors in adults, because carcinomas of the prostate, breast, lung, kidney, and thyroid often spread to the red marrow of the axial skeleton. Prostate cancer causes osteoblastic (sclerotic) lesions by releasing factors that stimulate osteoblasts. Kidney, thyroid, and lung cancers cause mainly lytic lesions, and breast cancer often causes mixed lesions. Metastases can cause pathologic fractures, and lytic lesions often cause hypercalcemia.
whyNot: Renal cell carcinoma produces purely lytic, often expansile and very vascular bone metastases.
Thyroid carcinoma that spreads to bone causes lytic lesions.
Correct.
Lung cancer metastases to bone are mainly lytic.

questions.stem: The tumor arose in the metaphysis next to the distal femoral growth plate, where new bone is laid down on calcified cartilage. In a child with severe vitamin D deficiency, which of the following changes would be seen in this growth plate?
options: A thin proliferative zone with short, sparse chondrocyte columns
Early fusion of the growth plate with loss of the reserve zone
Thick cores of calcified cartilage retained within trabeculae
A wide, disorganized hypertrophic zone that fails to mineralize
approach: List the zones from epiphysis to metaphysis: reserve, proliferative, hypertrophic, calcification, and ossification.
Vitamin D deficiency lowers calcium and phosphate, so cartilage matrix cannot calcify.
Hypertrophic chondrocytes are not cleared on time, so the plate widens and becomes irregular, which is rickets.
questions.why: In the growth plate, chondrocytes rest, divide in columns, swell in the hypertrophic zone, and then the matrix around them calcifies. Calcified cartilage is invaded by vessels and used as a scaffold for new bone in the metaphysis. In rickets, low calcium and phosphate prevent this calcification. Hypertrophic chondrocytes pile up, the plate becomes wide and disorganized, and the ends of the bones flare. In achondroplasia, by contrast, the proliferative zone is underactive.
whyNot: Too little chondrocyte proliferation is seen in achondroplasia, where activating FGFR3 mutations slow the proliferative zone.
Early closure of the growth plate follows excess estrogen, as in precocious puberty, and limits final height.
Retained calcified cartilage within trabeculae happens when osteoclasts cannot resorb it, as in osteopetrosis.
Correct.

case: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 1-week history of vaginal bleeding and a mass protruding from the vagina. Physical examination shows a soft, polypoid, grapelike mass at the vaginal opening. Biopsy shows a dense layer of primitive tumor cells just beneath the surface epithelium. Some tumor cells have abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm with cross-striations. The tumor cells stain for desmin and myogenin. Diagnosis: embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, botryoid type (sarcoma botryoides).

questions.stem: The pathologist also considered alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma, which is more common in the extremities of adolescents. Which of the following genetic findings would indicate the alveolar type?
options: EWSR1 fused to FLI1
SS18 fused to SSX1, SSX2, or SSX4
COL1A1 fused to PDGFB
PAX3 or PAX7 fused to FOXO1
approach: Recall the two main types of rhabdomyosarcoma in children: embryonal (younger children, head and neck or genitourinary tract) and alveolar (older children, extremities).
The alveolar type is defined by a fusion of a PAX gene with FOXO1.
Match each other fusion to its sarcoma to rule it out.
questions.why: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood. The embryonal type affects young children, often in the head and neck or genitourinary tract, and its botryoid form grows as grapelike masses under the mucosa of hollow organs such as the vagina and bladder. The alveolar type affects adolescents, often in the extremities, and carries PAX3 or PAX7 fused to FOXO1 from t(2;13) or t(1;13). Both types stain for desmin and myogenin, which mark skeletal muscle differentiation.
whyNot: This fusion from t(11;22) defines Ewing sarcoma, a CD99-positive small round cell tumor that lacks myogenin.
This fusion from t(X;18) defines synovial sarcoma, a soft tissue sarcoma of young adults near large joints.
This fusion drives dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, a slow-growing sarcoma of the dermis.
Correct.

questions.stem: The tumor cells resemble embryonic skeletal myoblasts. In normal development, the deep intrinsic muscles of the back arise from which part of the somite, and which nerves supply them?
options: Hypaxial myotome, supplied by dorsal rami
Epaxial myotome, supplied by ventral rami
Epaxial myotome, supplied by dorsal rami
Sclerotome, supplied by ventral rami
approach: Recall that somites divide into sclerotome, myotome, and dermatome.
The myotome splits into a dorsal epaxial part and a ventral hypaxial part.
Epaxial muscles become the deep back muscles and are supplied by dorsal rami of spinal nerves.
questions.why: Somites form from paraxial mesoderm and divide into sclerotome, which forms the vertebrae and ribs, myotome, which forms skeletal muscle, and dermatome, which forms the dermis of the back. The epaxial part of the myotome forms the deep (intrinsic) back muscles, supplied by dorsal rami. The hypaxial part forms the muscles of the body wall and limbs, supplied by ventral rami. Rhabdomyosarcoma cells copy this myoblast program, which is why they express desmin and myogenin even in sites such as the bladder and vagina, whose walls are made of smooth muscle.
whyNot: Hypaxial myotome forms the body wall and limb muscles, and these are supplied by ventral rami.
Epaxial muscles are supplied by dorsal rami. Ventral rami supply the hypaxial muscles of the body wall and limbs.
Correct.
Sclerotome forms the vertebrae and ribs, not muscle.

questions.stem: Her mother developed breast cancer at age 31 years, and a maternal uncle had adrenocortical carcinoma at age 8 years. Germline testing of the child is most likely to show a loss-of-function mutation in which of the following genes?
options: TP53
RB1
BRCA1
APC
approach: Look at the family pattern: several different cancers at young ages in one maternal line.
Childhood sarcoma, early breast cancer, and adrenocortical carcinoma are the core cancers of Li-Fraumeni syndrome.
Li-Fraumeni syndrome is caused by germline loss of TP53.
questions.why: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is an autosomal dominant cancer syndrome caused by germline TP53 mutations. p53 normally senses DNA damage and halts the cell cycle in G1 through p21 or triggers apoptosis. Without it, damaged cells keep dividing and gain more mutations. Affected families have soft tissue sarcomas such as rhabdomyosarcoma, osteosarcoma, early breast cancer, brain tumors, leukemia, and adrenocortical carcinoma, often in childhood or young adulthood.
whyNot: Correct.
Germline RB1 loss causes hereditary retinoblastoma and later osteosarcoma. It does not explain early breast cancer and childhood adrenocortical carcinoma.
BRCA1 raises the risk of breast and ovarian cancer but not childhood adrenocortical carcinoma or rhabdomyosarcoma.
APC loss causes familial adenomatous polyposis with hundreds of colon polyps.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman is found to have a large retroperitoneal mass. Biopsy shows intersecting fascicles of spindle cells with blunt-ended, cigar-shaped nuclei. Which of the following immunostaining profiles is most likely in this woman's tumor?
options: Desmin and myogenin positive, smooth muscle actin negative
Smooth muscle actin and desmin positive, myogenin negative
CD99 positive, desmin and myogenin negative
S100 and SOX10 positive, desmin negative
approach: Recognize spindle cells with cigar-shaped nuclei in the retroperitoneum of an older adult as leiomyosarcoma.
Leiomyosarcoma shows smooth muscle markers: smooth muscle actin and desmin.
Myogenin is a skeletal muscle transcription factor, present in rhabdomyosarcoma and absent in leiomyosarcoma.
questions.why: Leiomyosarcoma is a malignant smooth muscle tumor of adults that arises most often in the uterus and retroperitoneum. Its spindle cells have blunt, cigar-shaped nuclei and stain for smooth muscle actin and desmin. Desmin is found in both smooth and skeletal muscle, so myogenin, a skeletal muscle transcription factor, is the marker that separates rhabdomyosarcoma from leiomyosarcoma. Both sarcomas spread mainly through the blood, most often to the lungs.
whyNot: This profile marks skeletal muscle differentiation, as in the child's rhabdomyosarcoma.
Correct.
Strong CD99 without muscle markers suggests Ewing sarcoma, a small round cell tumor of young people.
S100 and SOX10 mark nerve sheath tumors and melanoma, which do not show muscle differentiation.

dx: Staphylococcus aureus septic arthritis of the knee in rheumatoid arthritis
case: A 64-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of severe pain and swelling of the right knee. She has had rheumatoid arthritis for 15 years and takes methotrexate and prednisone 7.5 mg daily. One week ago she had a draining, infected skin ulcer over her right ankle. She has had no joint injections or surgery. Her temperature is 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. The right knee is hot and swollen with a large effusion, and passive motion causes severe pain. Blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in clusters that are coagulase positive. Diagnosis: Staphylococcus aureus septic arthritis of the right knee.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how infection became established in this joint?
options: Bacteremia seeding a synovium damaged by inflammation
Deposition of staphylococcal antigen and antibody complexes
Spread from osteomyelitis of the adjacent distal femur
Direct inoculation through a penetrating wound of the knee
approach: Identify the likely source: an infected skin ulcer with Staphylococcus aureus now in the blood.
Most septic arthritis comes from hematogenous seeding, and the vascular synovium has no limiting basement membrane.
Rheumatoid arthritis adds risk through damaged, inflamed synovium and through immunosuppressive drugs.
questions.why: Most septic arthritis in adults results from bacteremia. Synovial capillaries are rich and lack a limiting basement membrane, so circulating bacteria can enter the joint. Joints already damaged by rheumatoid arthritis are especially vulnerable, and methotrexate and glucocorticoids weaken host defense. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause overall, and its adhesins for collagen and fibronectin help it attach in the joint. Other risk factors are prosthetic joints, injection drug use, and diabetes.
whyNot: Correct.
Immune complex deposition causes a sterile arthritis, as in SLE or serum sickness. Here live bacteria are growing in the blood.
Contiguous spread from bone does occur, but nothing in her history or exam suggests femoral osteomyelitis.
Direct inoculation follows trauma, surgery, or joint injection. She had none of these.

questions.stem: Arthrocentesis of the right knee is performed. Which of the following synovial fluid findings is most likely?
options: WBC 1,100/mm3, 20% neutrophils, no crystals
WBC 14,000/mm3, 70% neutrophils, no crystals
WBC 22,000/mm3, 85% neutrophils, needle-shaped crystals
WBC 96,000/mm3, 95% neutrophils, no crystals
approach: Recall the synovial fluid categories by WBC count: normal under 200/mm3, noninflammatory under 2,000, inflammatory 2,000 to about 50,000, septic usually over 50,000.
Septic fluid is dominated by neutrophils and has no crystals; Gram stain and culture are often positive.
In a patient with rheumatoid arthritis, a very high count separates infection from a flare.
questions.why: Synovial fluid analysis sorts an acute hot joint into categories. Normal fluid has fewer than 200 WBC/mm3, noninflammatory fluid fewer than 2,000, and inflammatory fluid from rheumatoid arthritis or crystals usually 2,000 to 50,000. Septic fluid usually has more than 50,000 WBC/mm3, mostly neutrophils, and Gram stain or culture is often positive. Crystal analysis is always done, because gout and infection can occur together.
whyNot: This is a noninflammatory fluid, under 2,000 WBC/mm3, as in osteoarthritis or trauma.
This is an inflammatory fluid, as in a rheumatoid arthritis flare. It is too low for a typical bacterial joint infection.
Needle-shaped crystals, negatively birefringent under polarized light, mean gout.
Correct.

questions.stem: The orthopedic team drains the joint urgently. If drainage is delayed, which of the following mechanisms will most directly cause rapid loss of her articular cartilage?
options: Osteoclast resorption driven by synovial RANKL
Urate crystals activating the NLRP3 inflammasome
Proteases and oxidants released by neutrophils
Antibody-dependent killing of chondrocytes
approach: Recognize that a septic joint fills with huge numbers of neutrophils.
Neutrophils release elastase, collagenases, matrix metalloproteinases, and reactive oxygen species.
These enzymes digest the cartilage matrix within days, along with bacterial toxins and enzymes.
questions.why: In septic arthritis, bacteria trigger a massive influx of neutrophils into the joint. Neutrophils release elastase, collagenases, and other proteases and reactive oxygen species. Avascular articular cartilage cannot repair itself, so its collagen and proteoglycans are destroyed within days. Pressure from the effusion also reduces blood flow to the joint. Prompt drainage and antibiotics are needed to save the joint.
whyNot: RANKL-driven osteoclasts cause the slow bone erosions of rheumatoid arthritis over months, not cartilage loss within days.
Urate crystals activate the NLRP3 inflammasome and IL-1 beta release in gout. No crystals are involved in this infection.
Correct.
Antibodies against chondrocytes are not the mechanism of joint destruction in bacterial infection.

questions.stem: The aspirated fluid is thin and watery and lacks the stringy quality of normal synovial fluid. Which of the following cells and secreted molecules normally give synovial fluid its viscosity?
options: Macrophage-like synoviocytes secreting chondroitin sulfate
Fibroblast-like synoviocytes secreting hyaluronan
Chondrocytes secreting type II collagen
Mast cells secreting heparin
approach: Recall the two cell types of the synovial lining: macrophage-like type A cells and fibroblast-like type B cells.
Type B cells secrete hyaluronan and lubricin into the joint space.
Hyaluronan makes the fluid viscous; in septic fluid, neutrophil enzymes and reactive oxygen species break it down.
questions.why: Synovial joints are lined by a synovial membrane with two cell types. Macrophage-like type A synoviocytes remove debris, and fibroblast-like type B synoviocytes secrete hyaluronan and lubricin. Hyaluronan, a long glycosaminoglycan, gives the fluid its viscosity, and lubricin lowers friction between cartilage surfaces. Synovial fluid also feeds the avascular articular cartilage. In septic arthritis, enzymes and oxidants break down hyaluronan, so the fluid loses its viscosity.
whyNot: Macrophage-like (type A) synoviocytes clear debris from the joint. Chondroitin sulfate is a proteoglycan side chain of cartilage matrix, not the main viscous molecule of synovial fluid.
Correct.
Chondrocytes make the collagen and proteoglycans of articular cartilage, which stay in the cartilage matrix.
Mast cells contain heparin, but it does not give synovial fluid its viscosity.

dx: Disseminated gonococcal infection with septic arthritis of the wrist
case: A 22-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 5-day history of fever and joint pain. The pain moved between her knees, elbows, and wrists and is now in her right wrist, which has become swollen. She has a new sexual partner and has no genital symptoms. Her temperature is 38.2 °C (100.8 °F). Physical examination shows a swollen, warm right wrist and pain along the dorsal wrist tendons with finger movement. There are four small pustules on red bases on her forearms and ankles. Synovial fluid from the wrist has 48,000 WBC/mm3 (normal under 200), 90% neutrophils, and no crystals; Gram stain is negative. Nucleic acid amplification testing of the fluid detects Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Diagnosis: disseminated gonococcal infection with septic arthritis.

questions.stem: She was treated for gonococcal cervicitis 18 months ago. Which of the following properties of the organism best explains why that infection did not protect her from this one?
options: A polysaccharide capsule that resists opsonization
Superantigen-induced anergy of helper T cells
Survival within phagolysosomes of macrophages
Antigenic variation of its pilus proteins
approach: Ask why a person can get gonorrhea again after infection.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae keeps changing its surface proteins, so antibodies from the last infection do not recognize the new strain.
Its pili undergo antigenic variation by gene recombination.
questions.why: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative diplococcus that attaches to mucosa with pili. By recombining silent pilin genes into the expressed site, it keeps changing the antigenic makeup of its pili, and it also varies its Opa proteins. Antibodies made during one infection therefore do not block the next, so reinfection is common and there is no vaccine. IgA protease cleaves mucosal IgA and helps the organism attach. Disseminated infection causes the triad of tenosynovitis, pustular skin lesions, and migratory polyarthralgia, or a purulent monoarthritis.
whyNot: Neisseria gonorrhoeae has no polysaccharide capsule. Neisseria meningitidis does, and vaccines target it.
Superantigens are made by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes, not by gonococci.
Intracellular survival in macrophages is the strategy of organisms such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Arthrocentesis of the right radiocarpal joint is performed from a dorsal approach. Which of the following carpal bones form the main articular surface that meets the distal radius in this joint?
options: Scaphoid and lunate
Lunate and pisiform
Scaphoid and trapezium
Capitate and hamate
approach: Recall the proximal row from lateral to medial: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform.
The distal radius articulates with the scaphoid and lunate.
The triquetrum meets the articular disc of the ulna, not the radius directly.
questions.why: The radiocarpal (wrist) joint is formed by the distal radius and the articular disc above, and the scaphoid, lunate, and triquetrum below. The distal radius itself articulates with the scaphoid and lunate, while the triquetrum contacts the articular disc. The ulna does not articulate directly with the carpal bones. A fall on an outstretched hand transmits force from the scaphoid to the radius, which explains why scaphoid and distal radius fractures are common.
whyNot: Correct.
The pisiform lies on the palmar surface of the triquetrum and does not reach the radius.
The trapezium is in the distal row. It articulates with the scaphoid and the first metacarpal, not with the radius.
The capitate and hamate are in the distal row and take part in the midcarpal and carpometacarpal joints.

topics: Carpal bones and the wrist joint

questions.stem: Early in her illness, pain at the radial side of the wrist was reproduced when she made a fist over her flexed thumb and the wrist was bent toward the ulnar side, and de Quervain tenosynovitis was considered. Inflammation of which of the following tendons produces that sign?
options: Extensor pollicis longus and extensor indicis
Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis
Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
Flexor carpi radialis and flexor digitorum superficialis
approach: Recognize the maneuver as the Finkelstein test, which stretches the tendons of the first dorsal compartment.
The first dorsal compartment holds the abductor pollicis longus and the extensor pollicis brevis.
Pain over the radial styloid with this test means de Quervain tenosynovitis.
questions.why: De Quervain tenosynovitis is inflammation and thickening of the sheath of the first dorsal compartment, which holds the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis at the radial styloid. Repetitive thumb and wrist use and late pregnancy or new parenthood are common settings. Folding the thumb into the palm and bending the wrist toward the ulna (Finkelstein test) stretches these tendons and reproduces pain. Gonococcal tenosynovitis, by contrast, is an infection and comes with fever and skin lesions.
whyNot: These tendons run in the third and fourth dorsal compartments. The extensor pollicis longus can rupture after distal radius fractures.
These wrist extensors share the second dorsal compartment and do not move the thumb, so the Finkelstein maneuver does not mainly stress them.
Correct.
These are flexors on the palmar side of the wrist. Ulnar deviation with the thumb in the fist stretches the radial-side extensors, not these.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most likely original site of the infection that spread to her wrist?
options: Pustular lesions on the distal extremities
Asymptomatic endocervical infection
Dorsal tendon sheaths of the wrist
Osteomyelitis of the distal radius
approach: Recall that gonococci first infect mucosa: cervix, urethra, rectum, or pharynx.
Mucosal infection in women is often silent, which lets bacteria reach the blood before treatment.
Bacteremia then seeds the joints, tendon sheaths, and skin.
questions.why: Disseminated gonococcal infection starts as a mucosal infection, most often of the cervix in women, that is frequently asymptomatic. Gonococci invade the bloodstream and seed tendon sheaths, skin, and joints. Most septic arthritis arises this way, by hematogenous seeding of the vascular synovium, rather than by direct inoculation. In sexually active young adults, Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a leading cause of septic arthritis, while Staphylococcus aureus dominates in older adults and those with damaged joints.
whyNot: The skin pustules come from bacteria spread through the blood. They are a result of dissemination, not its source.
Correct.
Tenosynovitis is part of disseminated infection. The tendon sheaths were seeded from the blood.
Contiguous spread from bone is a rare route here, and nothing suggests radial osteomyelitis.

dx: Type II necrotizing fasciitis from Streptococcus pyogenes
case: A 34-year-old previously healthy man comes to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of severe pain in the left lower leg. Two days ago he scraped his shin while playing soccer. His temperature is 39.4 °C (102.9 °F), pulse is 124/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 88/52 mm Hg. The anterior left leg is swollen and tense, with dusky red skin and several bullae. Pain is far greater than the skin changes suggest, and the skin is numb at the center. Serum creatinine is 2.1 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3). At surgery, the fascia is gray and necrotic and separates easily from the overlying tissue. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in chains, and culture grows beta-hemolytic group A streptococci. Diagnosis: type II necrotizing fasciitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why his pain was far greater than the visible skin changes early in the illness?
options: Infection of dermal lymphatics with a raised sharp border
Toxin cleavage of desmoglein 1 in the upper epidermis
Infection spreading along deep fascia under intact skin
Clostridial gas dissecting through skeletal muscle
approach: Place the infection: necrotizing fasciitis spreads along the deep fascia, beneath the skin.
The skin looks almost normal at first while vessels and nerves in the deeper layer are destroyed.
Later, thrombosis of perforating vessels causes dusky skin, bullae, and numbness from nerve death.
questions.why: Necrotizing fasciitis spreads quickly along fascial planes, which have a poor blood supply. Early on the skin over the infection looks almost normal, so severe pain is out of proportion to the exam. As bacteria and toxins cause thrombosis of the vessels that perforate the fascia, the skin becomes dusky, forms bullae, and loses sensation as nerves die. Type I is polymicrobial and common in diabetes and the perineum (Fournier gangrene); type II is caused by Streptococcus pyogenes, often in healthy people after minor injury. Crepitus is more typical of type I with gas-forming organisms.
whyNot: Infection of the upper dermis and lymphatics with a sharp, raised border is erysipelas. It is painful, but the visible skin changes match the pain.
Exfoliative toxin cleaving desmoglein 1 causes staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, with superficial peeling, not deep tissue destruction.
Correct.
Gas gangrene is a clostridial infection of muscle with crepitus. His Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in chains, not large gram-positive rods.

topics: Skin and soft tissue infection depth

questions.stem: He becomes more hypotensive despite fluids and develops a diffuse red rash. Which of the following actions of this organism's pyrogenic exotoxins best explains this shock?
options: Cleaving SNARE proteins to block release of neurotransmitters
Binding MHC II and T-cell receptors outside the peptide groove
ADP-ribosylating elongation factor 2 to stop protein synthesis
Inserting into cholesterol in host membranes to form large pores
approach: Recognize streptococcal toxic shock syndrome: shock and organ failure with an invasive group A streptococcal infection.
Pyrogenic exotoxins act as superantigens.
They link MHC class II to T-cell receptor V beta regions without processing, activating many T cells and causing a cytokine storm.
questions.why: Streptococcus pyogenes is a beta-hemolytic gram-positive coccus in chains. Its M protein resists phagocytosis by blocking complement deposition, and hyaluronidase and streptokinase help it spread through tissue planes. Its streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins are superantigens. They bind MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells and the V beta region of T-cell receptors outside the normal peptide groove, activating a large share of T cells at once. The resulting flood of IL-2, TNF-alpha, and IL-1 causes fever, capillary leak, shock, and organ failure.
whyNot: SNARE cleavage is how tetanus and botulinum toxins act. They paralyze rather than cause shock.
Correct.
This is how diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A kill cells, not the cause of streptococcal toxic shock.
Pore formation describes streptolysin O, which lyses cells and red blood cells but does not drive massive cytokine release.

questions.stem: During debridement, the surgeon opens the anterior compartment of the leg, which contains the dorsiflexors of the ankle. Which of the following developmental events explains why the extensor compartment of the leg lies anteriorly while the extensor compartment of the arm lies posteriorly?
options: Lateral rotation of the lower limb and medial rotation of the upper limb
Medial rotation of both limbs by about 90 degrees
Lateral rotation of both limbs by about 90 degrees
Medial rotation of the lower limb and lateral rotation of the upper limb
approach: Start with the early limb buds: flexor surfaces face ventrally and extensor surfaces face dorsally.
The upper limb rotates laterally about 90 degrees, so extensors end up posterior and the thumb lateral.
The lower limb rotates medially about 90 degrees, so extensors end up anterior and the big toe medial.
questions.why: Early limb buds have a ventral flexor surface and a dorsal extensor surface. In the seventh and eighth weeks the upper limb rotates laterally about 90 degrees, so its extensors face posteriorly and the elbow points back. The lower limb rotates medially about 90 degrees, so its extensors face anteriorly, the knee points forward, and the big toe lies medially. This medial rotation also twists the dermatomes of the leg into a spiral pattern.
whyNot: This reverses the true directions. If the lower limb rotated laterally, its extensors would face posteriorly like the arm's.
If both limbs rotated medially, both would have extensors facing anteriorly and thumbs facing medially.
If both limbs rotated laterally, both would have extensors facing posteriorly, which is not true of the leg.
Correct.

questions.stem: Over the following months, the scar over his leg is remodeled and gains tensile strength as the collagen first laid down in his granulation tissue is replaced. Which collagen type mainly replaces it?
options: Type I
Type II
Type III
Type IV
approach: Identify the early matrix: granulation tissue fibroblasts first make mostly type III collagen, the collagen of reticular fibers.
Remodeling degrades this collagen and replaces it with the collagen of dense connective tissue such as dermis, tendon, and ligament.
That strong, cross-linked fibrillar collagen is type I.
questions.why: Granulation tissue forms within days of injury and contains new capillaries, fibroblasts, macrophages, and a loose matrix. The first collagen deposited is mostly type III, the same type found in reticular fibers and vessel walls. During remodeling, matrix metalloproteinases break down this collagen and fibroblasts replace it with type I collagen, which is cross-linked to strengthen the scar. Even so, a mature scar reaches only about 70 to 80% of the strength of normal skin.
whyNot: Correct.
Type II collagen is found in hyaline cartilage and the nucleus pulposus, not in healing skin.
Type III collagen is the early collagen of granulation tissue. It is the collagen being replaced, not the replacement.
Type IV collagen forms basement membranes under the new epithelium and around vessels. It does not give a scar its tensile strength.
